newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa recovering after shock treatment.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa recovering after shock treatment.

text.p: A doctor who helped stabilise Mother Teresa's heartbeat with an electric shock on Wednesday said doctors might not be able to help the Roman Catholic nun if her heartbeat lapsed into an irregular rhythm again.

Dr Patricia Aubanel, a member of the panel treating Mother Teresa at Calcutta's B.M. Birla's Heart Research Centre, said she was well after the procedure but warned that the first 48 hours were critical.
"Still there can be some complication and her heart rhythm can turn chaotic again," Aubanel told reporters. "If it happens we will probably not be able to help her recovery."
Doctors will monitor the 86-year-old nun's condition closely for two days, she added. "Only after that will we be able to say she is out of danger."
Mother Teresa had heart surgery to clear two coronary artery blockages on November 29. Long-standing lung and kidney troubles complicated her recovery, coupled with an irregular heartbeat.
The lung and kidney problems have since been controlled. On Wednesday doctors corrected her heartbeat by administering a mild electric shock.
Earlier they had said they would first treat it with drugs, since Mother Teresa had expressed her reluctance to mechanical cardioversion, as the procedure is called.
"She was very happy," Aubanel said. "She did not object to mechanical cardioversion because she knew that it is very important for her recovery."
"The chances of having continuous regular rhythm are 50 percent," Aubanel said, replying to a question about the chances Mother Teresa's heart would return to its erratic rhythm.
"This means the chances of chaotic rhythm are 50 percent," Aubanel said. "She needs lots of support for several weeks."
Mother Teresa was optimistic.
Aubanel quoted her as saying she wanted to be fit by January when her Missionaries of Charity religious order meets to elect a new head.
"I have to be fully fit before the general chapter to be held in January," Aubanel quoted her as saying.
"We are trying and we are confident that you will be fully fit before the general chapter," Aubanel replied. "We are trying to send you home before Christmas."
Members of Mother Teresa's order meet every six years in a General Chapter, or secret ballot, to elect their chief, or superior-general, along with a four-member general council.

Mother Teresa may have to step down following health problems that have worsened since August, when she last had cardioversion. Doctors had postponed the procedure at the weekend so Mother Teresa could regain her strength.
They said the procedure, during which a shock pad attached to a machine was placed on Mother Teresa's chest, was carried out at 10:30 a.m. (0500 GMT).
"Is it over? Did it work?" Aubanel quoted Mother Teresa, who was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989 and has had three heart operations in five years, as asking after the procedure.
Told it was a success, Mother Teresa said: "Wonderful. Let us go home now."
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner underwent similar procedures in 1991 in the United States and in 1993 at the Birla clinic before her recent surgery.
